title: The problem with 5x5/3x5
summary: He explains why 5x5 and 3x5 work for novices (anything works while you are learning the movement) and why they fail afterwards. Matching reps across sets means sandbagging early sets, the fixed tonnage jumps lead to missed lifts and deloads, every lift gets the same scheme, and lifters never learn to handle plateaus. He recommends tight evolving rep ranges that keep roughly the same total reps.
claims: His favourite schemes are 1/3x2-5, 1/4x4-8, and 6-10, 8-12 and 10-15 rep ranges
Things that become staples become popular for a reason; humans recognise what works
5x5 and 3x5 (StrongLifts, Starting Strength) work for novices largely because anything works for novices
A novice's strength potential exceeds their neural ability to use it, so early bar gains are mostly technique learning and do not match muscle gained
Someone who adds a second 100 lb to their bench after the first gets far more muscle from that second 100 lb, because the learning phase is over
Beginners on these schemes can add 5 or even 10 lb to the bar per session for a long time
Results credited to 5x5 come from starting to train at all; almost any scheme short of something like 10x1 would have worked
The main flaw of 5x5/3x5 is that they never teach you to handle plateaus; deload-and-restart is just taking a longer run-up at the same wall
Stalling on 5x5 does not mean you hit your natural limit; it is the scheme's limitation, and it makes many people quit
Few people criticise 5x5 because most of YouTube fitness are beginners who quit or switch schemes and keep fond memories of it
He never ran 5x5 as a beginner and used evolving rep ranges from the start, though he admits 5x5 would have pushed him through the novice phase faster
5x5 catapults novices too fast into weights they should not be handling yet; they would benefit from spending longer as novices learning to program
Getting 5 reps on both the first and fifth set means you sandbagged the first set to survive the rest
Sets of 6-5-4 give the same tonnage as 5-5-5, but the first set reaches a higher intensity
Static rep schemes keep you off heavier weights until you master the current one for all sets, so you can stay stuck at a weight you could do for fewer reps
Static schemes reassure anxious novices and program authors avoid giving beginners freedom, but eventually you must accept that programming means thinking on your feet
The more flexible the program, the more tracking it needs and the more beneficial it is
One scheme applied to every lift ignores how differently lifts respond; a 5x5 squat and a 5x5 overhead press differ in fatigue, and the press stalls much faster
Fixed schemes make tonnage jump in big steps; when you miss, you must deload and land lower than where you started
People who progress on 5x5 for a very long time are gifted and would still do better on another scheme
He uses 5x4 only on lifts he does not care about progressing and that are fed by other specific lifts, as a mental break from evolving ranges
Using 5x5 on your main lifts in a minimalist program without variations shoots you in the foot twice
3x5 is better than 5x5 because matching reps over three sets involves less sandbagging and keeps you closer to failure
1x5 is great, 3x5 mediocre, 5x5 bad and something like 5x20 awful; fixed schemes are lazy programming
Replace 5x5 with an evolving range around the same 25 reps, such as 5x3-6 or 4x4-7 (16-28 reps)
Do not open an evolving rep range too wide; too much freedom lets tonnage dip, so keep it tight
He does only one to three working sets of strength work because his many variations and accessories supply the tonnage
